name: Nevada Current
title: Legislators could fix property tax, they ‘just don’t politically want to,’ says revenue chair
description: If Nevada lawmakers want to reform the state’s complicated and widely criticized property tax structure, a number of already vetted options are available. State Sen. Dina Neal (D-North Las Vegas) this week had the Legislature’s nonpartisan fiscal staff lay out several options to members of the interim committee on revenue, which she chairs. Neal said […]
text:
(Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)If Nevada lawmakers want to reform the state’s complicated and widely criticized property tax structure, a number of already vetted options are available.
State Sen. Dina Neal (D-North Las Vegas) this week had the Legislature’s nonpartisan fiscal staff lay out several options to members of the interim committee on revenue, which she chairs. Neal said she included the “educational only” presentation after hearing rumblings about the need for the state to conduct a study on property tax.
“We should not spend another hot dime, or six pennies, on another property tax study,” said Neal. “Because we know what the answer is. We just don’t politically want to do any of these solutions.”
Studies have already been commissioned and presented by the Guinn Center and Applied Analysis within the last decade.
Options that have been proposed in prior legislative sessions include adjusting the existing 3% cap on increases, creating a property tax that exists outside of the capped one, or resetting the assessed value when a property is sold.
Property tax is not a major contributor to the state general fund, though it does contribute to the State Education Fund, according to Nakamoto. It is also one of the biggest sources of revenue for cities and counties.
Local leaders have for years made the case that Nevada’s property tax structure, which has kept tax burdens low for homeowners, comes at the grave expense of municipal services like law enforcement, firefighters, parks, libraries, and schools.
Sparks Mayor Ed Lawson, a longtime critic of the state’s property tax system, last year told lawmakers his city’s expenses increased 54% over five years while revenue went up only 16%.
“I challenge any of you to run any kind of government or business with those kinds of numbers,” he said.
Legislative Counsel Bureau fiscal analyst Michael Nakamoto on Thursday told legislators it is up to them to make value judgments and balance the competing forces at play.
“This is the reality of how property taxes work in this state,” he added.
In 2005, the Nevada State Legislature capped at 3% the amount an owner-occupied residential property’s tax bill could rise. Other properties were capped at 8%. Home values at the time were rising so rapidly that homeowners were facing property tax raises upwards of 20%.
Those caps, which are effectively tax abatements, are the limiter for lawmakers looking to increase property tax revenue, Nakamoto explained. The property tax rate itself could be raised, doubled or quadrupled even, but the amount people actually pay would not increase because of the cap.
An estimated $18.6 billion in property tax has been abated since 2007, according to an analysis by legislative staff.
Using his own three bed, three bath split-level in Reno as an example, Nakamoto detailed for lawmakers and the public how an owner-occupied home’s tax bill is determined in Nevada.
Then, Nakamoto estimated what he can expect to pay going forward under the current system, and what he would pay going forward if changes were adopted.
Under the state’s existing tax structure, he can expect to pay $1,873 in property taxes and have $1,711 abated in 2029. Without the abatement, he would owe $3,584. If Nevada lawmakers were to move the cap from 3% to 4%, he would pay $1,892 in property tax and have $1,693 abated in 2029.
If the cap was set at 5%, he’d pay $1,910. At 6%, he’d pay $1,928. And if the owner-occupied residential cap was 8% — the same as commercial properties — he’d pay $1,964.
The difference between the final tax bills under those scenarios is less than $100, though it would add up over time.
Nakamoto calculated that in 2039, under an 8% cap structure he’d pay $4,241 in property tax, whereas under the current structure, he can expect to pay $2,518.
And if lawmakers were to remove the abatement altogether, his tax bill in 2029 would be $3,584 — nearly double the abated prior year. If you zoom out to 2039, the tax bill would be $5,265.
Adjusting the 3% cap isn’t lawmakers only option.
The 2005 bill that established the cap also included language specifying that any new, separate tax on property enacted by the Legislature could exist outside of the partial abatement structure. That means lawmakers could impose a new tax and keep it from being abated.
Under that scenario, Nakamoto contemplated a new tax rate of 25-cents per $100 of assessed value that would not be subject to the 3% cap for the first year only. That would result in him paying $2,118 in property tax in 2029 — a 16.5% spike. But in subsequent years the tax burden would again rise by just 3%.
If lawmakers boldly got rid of the abatement entirely and increased the tax rate by 25-cents per $100 of assessed value, the tax burden on Nakamoto’s house would immediately go up to $3,829 — a 110.5% change.
Another option would be to leave the mechanics of the property tax structure as is but reset the depreciation and partial abatements upon the sale of the property.
Assemblymember Natha Anderson (D-Washoe) last year sponsored a resolution proposing amending the state constitution to do just that. It passed the Assembly mostly on party lines but was never put up for a Senate vote. (Lawmakers passed a similar resolution in 2017 but failed to pass it a second time in 2019. As a constitutional amendment, it would need to pass in two consecutive sessions and then go to voters for final approval.)
The impact of resetting at point of sale would be “fairly dramatic,” said Nakamoto, “especially on older properties.
Under that scenario, if Nakamoto sold his home in 2029, the new owners would pay $7,782 in property taxes — 327% more than he paid the year prior. But, as proponents of the proposal have argued, it would be their baseline and more closely reflect the current value of their home.
Legislators on the revenue committee did not discuss any of the proposals at great length after Nakamoto’s presentation. Neal noted that those conversations would likely come at a later date.
Previous efforts to adjust Nevada’s property tax structure have been met with heavy opposition from real estate developers and anti-tax groups. They’ve seen support from progressive groups, which argue the state is overly reliant on the regressive sales tax, and local governments, which would benefit most financially.
“The conversation around property taxes is at its heart about who pays, and in turn what is being provided,” said Andrew Clarke with the Nevada Revenue Coalition, which is pushing for the resurrection of Anderson’s resolution.
“Nevada’s property tax structure has failed to deliver affordable homes and essential services,” he said in a statement to the Nevada Current. “Institutional investors have come out on top in this system while local budgets have run dry. We look forward to ending this two-tiered system and delivering a budget that can offer affordable homes and essential funding to education, childcare, and Nevada’s many other competing needs.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Outgoing lawmaker fears private-school vouchers will haunt Tennessee
description: State Rep. Caleb Hemmer is leaving the Tennessee Legislature with the feeling he made a mark in just two terms but with major concern that lawmakers passed private-school voucher programs that will prove too costly for the state to stomach. While some Democrats aren’t allowed to pass any bills, Hemmer, a Nashville Democrat, passed a […]
text:
Rep. Caleb Hemmer, a Nashville Democrat retiring after two terms in office, calls the legislature's move to create private school vouchers "the single worst policy decision" of his time in office. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)State Rep. Caleb Hemmer is leaving the Tennessee Legislature with the feeling he made a mark in just two terms but with major concern that lawmakers passed private-school voucher programs that will prove too costly for the state to stomach.
While some Democrats aren’t allowed to pass any bills, Hemmer, a Nashville Democrat, passed a children’s mental health bill and another measure this year designating Nashville hot chicken as an official state food, while working on policy and budgeting behind the scenes and focusing on constituent needs. 
Yet his gun-storage bill designed to cut down on thefts went nowhere, as did a provision that would have shone a light on the state’s newest private-school voucher and put income limits on the program. 
Hemmer doesn’t think Republicans who enacted the state’s two private-school voucher programs have completely given up on public schools. But he considers it “very shortsighted and misguided policy.” 
Beyond that, he said, lawmakers who voted for the state’s two private-school programs are “more scared of the voucher lobby and Jeff Yass of Pennsylvania,” referring to the billionaire who pours money into political action committees — including Club For Growth — that focus solely on vouchers than worried about solid education policy.
“You either get in line or you pay for the crime, and they’ll spend millions of dollars against you,” he said. “I think it’ll go down as the single worst public policy decision we made during my term for sure. It’s not gonna improve outcomes. It’s not gonna make public schools better by any means. It just costs more money for the taxpayers.”
Tennessee won’t know how many new vouchers go to existing private school students

Besides giving out money, mainly to students who were enrolled already in private schools, the state requires few “accountability measures,” Hemmer pointed out. The legislature this year stripped any requirement that students receiving the “scholarship” vouchers take the state’s main achievement test, only a national test, meaning Tennessee has no way to compare students’ performance.
Gov. Bill Lee, who made them his main initiative over eight years, went “all-in” for vouchers “for better or worse,” Hemmer said. “I just fear it’s going to be for the worse. Think of all the things we can do in education policy that evidence has backed.”
Republican gubernatorial candidate U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, likely the next governor, is backing school “choice,” though she has shied away from saying she would expand it beyond the legally allowed number of 5,000 students annually. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jerri Green, a Memphis City Council member, is pledging to defund vouchers if elected.
In the backdrop
Indianapolis-based EdChoice Legal Advocates, a school “choice” group, has filed a motion to end an ACLU-backed challenge to the state’s newest private-school voucher program. 
A hearing is coming up in Davidson County Chancery Court where Jefferson County parent Denise Fair and her husband, both first responders, are seeking to intervene. They worked extra jobs to pay the tuition for their two youngest daughters to attend private schools, and the state funds have cut the burden.
“It has allowed me more time to dedicate to attending activities with the girls and freed up enough financial resources to allow the girls to attend some school field trips,” Denise Fair said in a statement.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
EdChoice is also representing Mike and Monica Sweeney of Knoxville, who rely on the money to send their children to a Catholic school after pulling them out of another school and homeschooling because of concerns about COVID-19 guidelines, according to a statement.
Their action comes in response to litigation by a group of 10 Tennessee parents and taxpayers who filed suit in November 2025 challenging the constitutionality of the state’s “universal” private-school voucher program, claiming it shifts funds to unaccountable private schools that “openly discriminate” against students.
In its first year, the program provided vouchers worth $7,300 to 20,000 students at a cost of $144 million, plus all the extras to entice passage. Lawmakers initially approved money for 10,000 students whose family incomes hit 300% of the federal subsidized lunch program, about $180,000, and 10,000 for students with no family income requirement.
Before even seeing how well it worked, lawmakers expanded the program this year to 35,000 students, pushing the cost above $260 million and the state’s total expense for private-school vouchers, including an initial program for low-income kids passed in 2019, well past the $300 million mark.
The fight might never end.
Senate Democrats pounced on the latest figures showing public school students receive less in state funding than private-school voucher students.
Their numbers show Lee and Republican lawmakers put $6.9 billion toward K-12 schools for this school year, $7,272 per student, about $260 less on average than those in the private-school voucher program receive, $7,530. Students in the Education Savings Account program receive even more from the state, roughly $9,000, even as their performance appears to be flagging.
Lawmakers took federal money under the Obama administration for the Race to the Top program, which some critics have referred to as the “Race Over the Edge,” turning an end-of-year test into the end-all-be-all of education.
Many teachers believe the move took the joy out of teaching, forcing them to “teach to the test” instead of focusing on fundamentals and expanding the mind (not through psychedelia). 
That view goes out the door, though, now that the state is pouring money into private schools.
And while lawmakers such as Hemmer want a better accounting of the number of private-school students who received the money, Lee made no secret he was writing a check for private-school kids and parents when they surrounded him during the Capitol bill-signing ceremony two years ago.
Even some of the state’s staunchest Republicans call it a “give-away.” But by the time the state hits a financial crisis because of this government expansion, it might be too late to turn back.
More historical accuracy, please
Page four of ” Marsha Blackburn Coloring Book An American Story,” depicts an idyllic version of life in the South. (Tennessee Lookout copy)
A new coloring book surfaced recently in support of Blackburn’s gubernatorial bid, displaying her in the idyllic setting of a Mississippi upbringing and, we might add, looking about 30 years younger. We’re told it wasn’t sanctioned by her campaign.
While it shows her wrapped in swaddling clothes, picnicking with the fam, going to school, helping others and visiting the local community theater, the coloring book leaves out a few minor details. It shows no “colored only” water fountains or segregated schools and theaters, nor does it mention the murders of three voter rights activists by the KKK in Neshoba County, Mississippi, which took place about the time Blackburn would have been 12 years old.
In short, while it mentions “Southern roots, strong values, and bright future,” the book glosses over the harsh reality of living in Mississippi and much of the South for Black Americans in the 1960s and ’70s. Then again, it is only a book that requires people to keep their colors within the lines.
Winning friends
Republican U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbarger introduced a federal bill Thursday that would have gone over well with Mayberry’s Morrison sisters, who used a “flower-making machine” to create their medicinal “elixir” on “The Andy Griffith Show.” (Admission: I had to look up their name.)
Steve Earle wants a word: Earle, center, singer and songwriter of “Copperhead Road,” a ditty about raising weed in East Tennessee, may approve of U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbargers’s move to legalize moonshining. Earle is pictured with House Speaker Cameron Sexton and Rep. Bo Mitchell. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Harshbarger is sponsoring the Freedom to Home Distill Act, which would do exactly what it says, end the prohibition on distilling spirits at home and provide the tax-free, personal-use exemption enjoyed by beer and wine brewers.
“Distilling has deep roots in Tennessee and across Appalachia, tied to self-reliance and craftsmanship that go back generations. It’s long past time we modernize this outdated federal law,” said Harshbarger, who hails from Kingsport.
“Moonshiners” TV series star Eric “Digger” Manes brought the idea to her, saying even the nation’s first president, George Washington, made moonshine.
“Given that multiple states have legalized marijuana, it appears logical that we should be permitted to engage in our hobby without facing repercussions,” Manes said in a statement.
Apparently, he didn’t run that statement by Tennessee’s top GOP lawmakers. But it’s a start. 
Of course, without the prohibition we wouldn’t have some of the state’s most popular tunes, one of which was sung on the state House floor.
“You hardly ever saw Grandaddy down here / He only come to town about twice a year / He’d buy a hundred pounds of yeast and some copper line / Everybody knew that he made moonshine.”*
*”Copperhead Road,” Steve Earle
